articles.title: HOW BELIEVERS PROVE THE LORD AS PRIEST
articles.author: J. Renton
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Plainfield, N.J.

paragraphs.text: The Epistle to the Hebrews is a very important one. Of course all the epistles are important, but there is something special about the Epistle to the Hebrews. As far as I can remember it is the only scripture in the New Testament which presents the Lord Jesus as Priest. This epistle was written to Hebrew Christians, and no doubt Paul wrote it, and he wrote it in language which they would understand. In John 6 Peter came to it that Jesus was the holy One of God, and that would involve His priesthood, but I do not think the Lord is definitely called Priest in any other New Testament scripture. That, of itself, would make the epistle very important because the priesthood of Christ is a truth that we all need to understand and appreciate.

Now in these two scriptures I have read we get reference to the kind of persons who get the full benefit of the Lord’s priesthood. The Lord Jesus as Priest would have every believer on His heart. The high priest in the Old Testament wore the breastplate which contained the names of each of the tribes of Israel, and even if the tribe was not what it ought to be, its name was still there. The Lord Jesus is available as Priest to every believer, but we read where He “does not indeed take hold of angels by the hand, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham”. Now “the seed of Abraham” would suggest the moral features that characterised Abraham, therefore the Lord taking hold of the seed of Abraham means that the Lord Jesus supports as Priest persons who are characteristically obedient and believing and are here for the will of God. Even if believers are not devoted to the will of God the Lord Jesus has regard for them and is available for them, but it is persons who are committed to the will of God who get the full support of the Priest. It may be that the Lord as Priest is not known as He ought to be. I believe that when brothers and sisters get older and maybe weak in body, maybe suffering, such persons experience the Lord as Priest. Even if they do not realise that it is as Priest that they are looking to Him, in experience they draw support and are strengthened and are able to overcome frailty, and in spirit they are able to rise above weakness. That is the believer drawing from the Priest; it is the Lord’s priestly grace and support that enable believers to rise above infirmity or suffering, or whatever it may be.

Now such are of the seed of Abraham. Abraham did not take an easier path. There might be, as we have had in our meetings, a tendency with us to take an easier path, to look for an easier way, a way that would involve less exercise, less sacrifice, but that was not the way Abraham took. Abraham took the path of obedience and believing God. It says in this very epistle, “By faith Abraham, being called, obeyed to go out into the place which he was to receive for an inheritance, and went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11: 8).

He stepped out in faith, but he was supported and sustained and helped. Melchisedec met him and brought forth bread and wine to support him and sustain him in this way of the will of God. He went out, not knowing where he was going. All Abraham knew was the God who called him; and he trusted Him and took the step in faith, not seeing the end of the way.

Abraham was the first to be called and, remarkable man that he was, he went out not knowing where he was going. We have a whole chapter, the eleventh of Hebrews, to show those who were in this way before

us. Our Lord Jesus Himself is presented in chapter twelve as the Leader and Completer of faith. He sets out the whole course. This book speaks about the race, the course; the Lord Jesus is our Forerunner and we are after-runners in the same course as He fulfilled, and I need not say it was no easy path. It was a path of suffering and reproach and sorrow. He was a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief and, as this passage indicates, He went through these experiences that He might, speaking reverently, qualify to enter sympathetically into the feelings that believers have as they follow their Forerunner; as we had on Lord’s day, ‘We follow our Forerunner to His God’ (Hymn 284). We are not stepping out into the dark, because the Lord Jesus has gone before us, besides all these persons who are mentioned in chapter 11. We are thus assured of the end of the way we undertake.

The seed of Abraham would suggest persons who down here from day to day are committed to the will of God, and they know they can draw from the succour and sympathy and support of the Lord Jesus in His grace as Priest. No matter what is involved in it, and sometimes there is a great deal of sorrow and heart-rending involved, there is One, dear brethren, whom we can draw from who has known sorrows such as we shall never know. One who has suffered as we shall never suffer. We are assured of His succour and His ability to strengthen us in our day-to-day path down here. “For he does not indeed take hold of angels by the hand, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham”: in this sense He would take hold of us by the hand. You remember in Matthew 14 Peter stepped out of the boat and began to walk on the waters to go to Jesus. He could not sustain the walking on the water but began to sink, but he said, “Lord, save me”, and Jesus stretched out His hand and caught hold of him. He does not take hold of angels by the hand, but He takes hold of the seed of Abraham.
Peter was, in principle, of the seed of Abraham. He had right desires. He was attracted and attached to the Lord, for He was his object, but he needed to be taken hold of by the hand of the Priest.

That is a kind of illustration of the believer’s path down here. Sometimes we are confronted with sorrows and difficulties, troubles that seem impossible to face. We have not the strength to face them, but in the assurance of the support of our Lord Jesus as Priest, in His sympathy, His love and grace, His faithfulness, we are able to go through as taken hold of by the hand. It says, “Wherefore it behoved him in all things to be made like to his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest”. He is merciful and faithful. It is remarkable how it is put.
It does not say ‘faithful and merciful’; it is “merciful and faithful”. Think of the mercy, the grace, the tenderness of the Priest we have. He is faithful, of course, but then He is merciful.

He will consider for us in every way and support us, especially as we are here for the will of God, involving some cost and some sacrifice on our part. It says “in that himself has suffered, being tempted, he is able to help those that are being tempted”. This epistle speaks about the Lord being made perfect through sufferings (Hebrews 2: 10) as the Leader of our salvation, and salvation in this epistle would be a full matter, a daily matter. The Lord is available for every one of His own inasmuch as the twelve tribes were on the breastplate of the high priest.

Not only does the breastplate suggest believers individually, but inasmuch as there were twelve tribes it might suggest localities. The Lord Jesus is able to save us, to support us, individually and also to support and strengthen and sustain us in all our local exercises as we are committed to His will as being of the seed of Abraham.

Now in Hebrews 7 the same persons who are referred to as of the seed of Abraham are spoken of as those “who approach by him to God”; “Whence also he is able to save completely those who approach by him to God, always living to intercede for them”. They are those who approach by Him to God, which would involve that they are for God’s pleasure. It would involve what we speak of as the service of God. Believers are meant to be down here committed to the will of God and they are meant to be persons who are available for the great matter of the service of God. The first seven chapters in this epistle, as we have been taught, refer to the Priest as Minister of the holy places, who sustains the service of God and those who approach by Him to God. The Lord said when He was here, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father unless by me”, John 14: 6. That must include His priesthood. So the Lord’s priesthood leads on to His being Minister of the holy places as Priest, as Aaron was in the Old Testament. He was for the people, but he was also minister and sustained the whole service of God in the tabernacle system. Let us be persons, therefore, who are here in day-to-day life, committed to the will of God in faith and obedience, as Abraham was, and let us be persons who are committed to be here in view of being available under the Lord’s hand for the service of God.

To be occupied with what God is doing in the present revival profits the soul and exhilarates the affections. He has recovered, and is still recovering, many persons to the light given through Paul, the distinctive light of this unique dispensation. Also He is working subjectively, by the Holy Spirit, in persons to conform them to the image of His Son, and in this way He is beautifying the house of His magnificence (Isaiah 60: 7). Let us not detract from the glory of the assembly as the house of God’s magnificence, for to do so is regarded seriously by God (Micah 2: 9).

When John the baptist got somewhat dull he sent two of his disciples to Jesus to enquire, “Art thou he that is coming, or are we to wait for another?” Jesus did not say, ‘Tell him I am He’. No, He told them to tell John about what was happening in persons, Luke 7: 22. No doubt that would cheer John. So as we are engaged with the glory of what God is doing in His saints at the present time for His own pleasure and satisfaction then we are brightened in our spirits, we are exhilarated in our affections, and enlarged spiritually (Isaiah 60: 5).
Lossiemouth

I seek to speak, dear brethren, from this scripture in relation to the matter of recovery. We speak a good deal of recovery in relation to persons who return to the Lord in these days. We are thankful for every one of them, and we would be constant in our prayers that more may be added to

their number. We are indeed all recovered persons. Man has got away from God; we have all had to retrace our steps from having “turned every one to his own way”, and we have found that “Jehovah hath laid upon him the iniquity of us all”, Isaiah 53: 6. But recovery is to the highest truth, which remains even in this day. It is a tribute to the service of the blessed Holy Spirit that there is here on earth at the present time that which the Lord Jesus can take account of.

It says in John 20: 19 that “Jesus came and stood in the midst”. There is that to which He can come in the light of the whole universal position, in the light of the assembly as it is on earth at the present time. We do not speak of that as a matter of theory, but as something which is very real, which we have proved by experience. We know what it is for the Lord Jesus to come in where the doors are shut. We know what it is for Him to say, “Peace be to you”, and to be sent out into the testimony from an area of privilege where we have experienced such intimate relations with Himself. These things are real, and they are there for persons to be recovered to them in these last days.

Perhaps we have not thought sufficiently of the meaning of that word ‘recovery’. It is not only that persons return—that is their side of the matter—but the question on our side is whether we can bring persons back. James speaks of one who brings a person back, and covers a multitude of sins.

Well, we must begin from the top, and see the way in which divine Persons have operated in recovery. We have experienced it as set out in this chapter, which has been used in the preaching of the gospel for hundreds of years now—how God has moved out from His own side to bring us back. There was nothing in the way of movement back on the

part of the lost sheep, but the shepherd went after it. With the lost drachma there was the sweeping of the house that it might be brought to light. And then it was the father who covered the distance. That is why I went from verse 13 to verse 20. The younger son went into a country “a long way off”, and while he was yet a long way off his father saw him. His father could cover that great distance, and could embrace him, and call for him to be clothed in that which suited him to have part in the merriment and rejoicing which was to proceed in the house because of the recovered son.

The question for us, as we contemplate these things and consider them together, is as to what part we can have in these activities. How do they take place at the present time? We know what was involved in this for Jesus—leaving the ninety and nine in the wilderness and going after that which was lost until He found it. Think of where He has been for each one of us, where He has been to find us. Paul sets it out so clearly—“that one died for all, then all have died”, 2 Corinthians 5: 14. He reached us where we were, dead in offences and sins, and He went into death to reach us. That was how far He went, and as the hymn says,
‘But none of the ransomed ever knew
How deep were the waters crossed,
Nor how dark was the night that the Lord passed through Ere He found His sheep that was lost’.

Think of the way He has been, beloved, to reach you and to reach me. That is the way He has moved in recovery so that man might be brought back to God, so that man might be once again for God’s pleasure.
I was impressed with the simple word here “my lost sheep”. Think of the value which the Lord Jesus has set upon each one of us—upon you and upon me. If you are the youngest here, you may

feel you have a very small part in these things and have not gone very far on the road, but the Lord Jesus values you so much that He was prepared to go all that way to reach you and to bring you back. How wonderful these words are—‘his own shoulders’. He did it all Himself—carried the whole load, the whole weight, so that you and I might be brought back.
He “suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God”, 1 Peter 3: 18.
Think of the load that He bore, so that He might bring us back, and how He values each one of us because we are His sheep.

This would lead us, I believe, to have a right valuation of one another. What valuation have we of one another? What valuation have we of our brethren who are not available to us? I say that in the widest sense, even as Mr. Darby could write to his ‘Roman Catholic brethren’

(Coll.Wrtgs. Vol.18, p.1). These brethren are lost for the time being, not only those we have once walked with, but so many in christendom. Who knows how many there are? “The Lord knows those that are his” (2 Timothy 2: 19), and we should be such that other people know that we are His. But then, as to these others, how far are we prepared to go to reach them?

How far was the Lord Jesus prepared to go to reach you, dear brother, and to reach me? I just say this suggestively, although I feel the edge of it myself, as not having gone very far in seeking others with a view to their recovery. When I think of how far He went, how far am I prepared to go? I believe an understanding of His own word “my lost sheep”—what they are to Him, and where He has been for each one—would encourage us. Paul could say—“The Son of God, who has loved me and given himself for me”, Galatians 2: 20. Think of what Jesus has given for each one of His own—every blood-bought saint on earth at the present time, the myriads of them, whether available to us or not. How far are we

prepared to go, as we take account of the immense value that He has put upon them, so that they might be recovered for His pleasure, and He would say, “Rejoice with me”? What joy it would give to the Lord Jesus if we were able to reach any and bring them back.

So it says that, “having found it, he lays it upon his own shoulders”. How much are we prepared to carry, dear brethren? Think of what Paul could speak of—all that pressed upon him daily. How much presses upon us daily in relation to the testimony? How much presses upon us as to those who are not available to us, with a view to their recovery? How much are we prepared to carry, so that others might be reached and brought in, available to the Lord, at the present time?

We must always bear in mind that Matthew gives us the teaching as to the assembly, and it says there, not that he left them in the wilderness, but that he left them on the mountains (Matthew 18: 12). We have to remember that. There are those who would go out and lower the standard of things, leaving the position which has been reached through the teaching in the recovery as to the assembly. So in Matthew, where the teaching of the assembly is, it would seem that recovery is more difficult, for it says—“If it should come to pass that he find it” (Matthew 18: 13). As taking assembly ground we have to realise that if we are to maintain the level which is due to the Lord in the assembly it is not going to be easy to recover persons and to bring them back to that level. So in Matthew he goes out from that elevation, and that is the level to which he would return, bringing them back to the mountains. Can we bring persons back to the mountains? Can we bring them back to the high level and standard of the truth to which we have been recovered ourselves, which has never been impaired by the breakdown? These glorious matters

which are coming before us now belong to the mountain-top. Are we holding them as such, so that we might bring persons up to that level, and how far are we prepared to go to find them? I raise the question with myself as much as with any, as to how this can work out at the present time.

It must be, of course, that the Lord goes before. We of ourselves can effect nothing by way of recovery. Verse 7 speaks of “one repenting sinner”. What makes the sinner repent? The Lord has worked there; the Lord Himself has gone before, and we would be concerned that He would let His work appear unto His servants, so that we might link on with what He is doing.
Apart from this, our work will come to nought.

Then there is the next section which gives in figure the service of the Holy Spirit, sweeping the house and seeking carefully, as it says of the woman, “till she find it”. Here it is a question of diligence, and it is within the area of the house. There may even be persons in fellowship, as we say, not vitally in circulation. Do we take account of the potential that is there for the divine pleasure? And do we use diligence in relation to them, having in view the value of “the assembly of God, which he has purchased with the blood of his own”, Acts 20: 28? Do we act like the beloved apostle there as he ceased not to admonish each one? Do we take account of those who are in the house, if I may apply it that way, but perhaps for the moment not vitally responsive because of some leaning towards the world or “earthly things”? Are we concerned to use diligence in relation to them, to rekindle the work that is in them, having in view their value to God? The drachma would remind us of the half shekel of the sanctuary—“the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less” (Exodus 30: 15)—and the value of every one to God for “the service of the
tent of meeting” (verse 16).

Well, the searching is the service of the Holy Spirit; we may be content to leave it there, but I believe we are to have part in the work. The Lord can, and does, work by Himself, even as He could arrest Saul of Tarsus by a voice out of heaven. We know, too, how He has spoken to each one of us. As I have said, it must be His own work, but there is that in which He would call us to have part at the present time. So also the Holy Spirit is acting sovereignly in persons, but He is pleased, in the infinite grace which marks Him, to use vessels who are available to Him in what He is doing—applying the word of God in its searching character so that more might be available to the Lord in view of the service of God and for His own joy.

Then we have this younger son who gathered all together and “went away into a country a long way off”. Oh how sad it is that some have done that! And the elder son was equally outside his father’s house, although so near. Do we know of persons who have gone into a country a long way off? Again I say, we are dependent upon the work of God. We can effect nothing of ourselves, but are we on the look-out? because it says—“While he was yet a long way off, his father saw him”. At the first sign of movement, “his father saw him ... and ran”.

Can we take account of any in whom God is working, who may be “yet a long way off”? And can we, as the father did, come in with a ministry of reconciliation so that the distance is removed? Again I say, without any sense of compromise or in any way lowering the standard, can we remove the distance? It says “his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell upon his neck, and covered him with kisses”.

Can we reflect the feelings of God—who “so loved … that he gave his only begotten Son”, John 3: 16? Are we rightly representing Him in relation to persons who may have got a long way off? Can we move towards them so that they might be brought back, and are we ready to clothe them so that they might be at liberty in the house? Think of how he clothed him, apart from anything else, by saying “This my son”. These persons who may have got away are never viewed by God apart from what they are as His sons, for He has given so much to secure them, and “the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin”, 1 John 1: 7.
They never cease to be what they are, so Paul says to the Galatians—“ Ye are all God’s sons by faith in Christ Jesus”, Galatians 3: 26. They had got into bondage, and gone back to
“beggarly principles”, like this son here. He got away into a beggarly position, but he never ceased to be a son. So the father could clothe him by saying, “This my son”.

Well, how do we regard our brethren who may have gone astray? Do we regard them in any lower light than what they are as of value in God’s sight? Can we not see that what has come to fruition in their going astray is in our own hearts, but through the grace of God alone we have been preserved? I believe that if we look at it that way we shall be helped to view them as God sees them, in the light of what they are to Him. Then we shall be able to bring in a ministry of reconciliation which will remove the distance. We see what God has done from His own side at such tremendous cost so that everything might be established on a righteous basis, a way of recovery secured, and persons brought into the merriment which is set on afresh as each repenting one returns.
So it says, “the father said to his bondmen, Bring out the best robe and clothe him in it, and

put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet; and bring the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and make merry—for this my son was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found”. Think of the joy that there is in heaven, as it says in the other two instances, “for one repenting sinner”. What joy there is for the heart of God in persons being recovered! I believe that would be the motive that would help us on this line, and would stimulate us as we would seek to be available under the hand of God in view of the recovery of persons for His service and praise. We feel for those in small numbers in isolation in other parts of the world. As you see them, your heart goes out for them as not having the privilege we have of gathering together for meetings such as this, their neighbours being thousands of miles away. How we should feel for them! Yet, thank God. His work is very real there, and we would be looking for recovery.

But what is the motive for this? How easy it is to look for increase for the sake of increase, but I believe that as we have these things before us we would have right motives in seeking to recover persons. We would remember that He says, “my lost sheep”; it is nothing that we can lay claim to; it is His, and He has laid claim to it, and laid down His life for it. We would not be as those who lord it over their possessions, but those who recognise that the assembly is the assembly of God which He has purchased with the blood of His own. We would recognise that persons are to be recovered to the full light and dignity of what God has in mind for them, and are those of whom He says “my son”—remembering what we have often been taught, that sonship is for God.
So let us take account, beloved, of the potential that there is all around us. Some we know, many we have never known, and many, I suppose, we shall never

know until we are united with them in glory. Let us have recovery in mind in relation to what is for God. Those who are recovered are to be available for Him at the present time. Let us be exercised as to how far we can go to find them. Let us be diligent to uncover that which is really of God, to bring it to light for His joy and pleasure. May we be encouraged to remove any distance which has come in by bringing in a ministry of reconciliation, and clothe persons with God’s thoughts for them, that they may be fully restored for His pleasure and praise.
Lord Jesus, we know Thee as living,
How well for Thine own Thou doss care;
On earth we are weak and are needy,
But know we can turn to Thee there.
We know how in love Thou suppliest
The grace for the need of the soul,
For Thou art the blessed Physician,
Thy touch it is maketh us whole.
We think of Thy grace that instructed
The minds of disciples of old,
Thus now we would seek understanding
Of all that Thou wouldest unfold.
*With Christ, July 1977
We sit at Thy feet, all attentive,
And learn from the Scriptures of Thee;
What wonderful things in its pages
We thus by the Spirit may see.

The Father would have us share His thoughts as to Christ. It is one of our greatest privileges to love Christ with the same character of love as the Father. This is very precious to the Lord Jesus too. How often we think of the Lord’s words in John 17 as He prays to the Father, “that the love with which thou hast loved me may be in them” (verse 26). We are thus intimately bound up with the Father and the Son. In that same prayer in John 17 the Lord asks “that they also may be one in us” (verse 21). It is a wonderful thought that we are intimately brought into the circle of divine affection, to share the Father’s love to the Son, to be with Christ before the Father, having the Father’s Spirit and the Spirit of Jesus. How exalted the privileges of christianity are! In our first scripture the Father says, “This is my beloved Son”.

In our second scripture it is, “my servant”, and in Psalm 2, “my king”. In each case it is God claiming Christ and giving us to understand His love to Him in whom everything is headed up for His pleasure and who at such cost has secured everything for Him.
In Matthew 17 it was a peculiar privilege for these three men. They are brought up into a high
mountain apart, apart from the world, far above the level of earth. They are three selected persons of the greatest distinction. One often thinks of the distinctiveness of the apostles.

They were the direct result of the work of Christ, as He said, “I will make you ...”, Mark 1: 17. We might say carefully that He took up the raw material and formed it into something very wonderful which we see in its fulness in the Acts as Peter and John say, “Look on us”.

They were men who had been with Jesus, who had been formed by Him, educated by Him, disciplined by Him; but they had also been in the greatest privilege with Him and had been initiated into divine secrets. There were also two men from the Old Testament, Moses and Elias. What men they were! But none is to be compared to Jesus. Peter would attempt to associate Moses and Elias on the same level as Jesus and there is immediately a divine intervention, “a bright cloud overshadowed them”. Peter speaks of it as “the excellent glory”; and there came a voice out of the cloud. Peter says, “such a voice being uttered to him”, 2
Peter 1: 17. He had never heard such a voice before, conveying all the power and depth of the Father’s love, poured out as it were in relation to the Person of Jesus.

Just before this the Lord had spoken of His sufferings. “From that time Jesus began to shew to his disciples that he must go away to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised” (Matthew 16: 21). The Lord was to move onward to death, but now is the point of His glorification. What those downward movements meant to the Father! We have His exact words here, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have found my delight”. There had been faithful men earlier—Moses is said to have been faithful in all His house; but every other man now recedes. It says in Matthew 17: 8,

“they saw no one but Jesus alone”. We are left just with the impression of the Father’s love to the Son. God had sent forth His Son; that moment had come, that supreme moment in the ways of God, and the Son was here in the perfection of His devoted service. We were speaking in the reading as to the bullock in Leviticus 8: 14; Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bullock, speaking of the mind which was in Christ Jesus (Philippians 2: 5). That mind was in perfect harmony with the Father’s will; as is said of Abraham and Isaac in Genesis 22, “they went both of them together”.

We contemplate this worshipfully—a divine Person in manhood in the most blessed intimacy with the Father. The Lord Himself says, “The Son can do nothing of himself save whatever he sees the Father doing—for whatever things he does, these things also the Son does in like manner. For the Father loves the Son and shews him all things which he himself does”, John 5: 19, 20. This is for our contemplation. What it meant to the Father to see the Son pursuing the path of His will, in His mind and heart the Father’s purposes cherished, and moving onward to death to secure them, every step taken in the dignity, devotion, and glory of sonship. Think of the Father’s holy and absolute confidence in this blessed Person as John records, “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things to be in his hand”, John 3: 35.

How infinitely trustworthy! Here was the One to whom the Father had committed all His pleasure; the whole wealth of eternal purpose depended on Jesus, as one of our hymns expresses it, ‘By Him the working out was all achieved’ (Hymn 5) We witness this scene in reverence to gather an impression of the Father’s supreme delight.
We see a divine Person here in manhood, on the one hand to undo all the works of the devil, but positively to bring in all that is for God’s pleasure, and to

establish it for time and eternity, and every thought and action is fragrant and delightful to the Father. So the Father says, “This is my beloved Son”. We must allow for what is the Father’s exclusively. There is what we share, but there is what is the Father’s alone; “No one knows the Son but the Father”, Matthew 11: 27. This would cause us to worship in the sense of what is infinite and inscrutable in divine relationships.

In Isaiah we have “my servant”. There had been many other servants. We think of such as Moses, David, Solomon, and the prophets. But this is the uniqueness of Christ as “my servant”. How wonderful that He should take a servant’s place, being found here indeed in a bondman’s form. We need to contemplate the manhood of Jesus and to feed upon it that we might be formed in this character. It says, “my servant whom I uphold, mine elect in whom my soul delighteth!” This is the Father’s view of Jesus day by day as here, devoted to the securing of the Father’s will in its glorious fulness and in every detail. “He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street”. There is nothing that would impress man as such, no natural forcefulness, but the fulness of divine power as upheld by God, and the Spirit upon Him, as He Himself said, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4: 18), and again, “If I by the Spirit of God cast out demons ... “, Matthew 12: 28. So Paul says, “God was in Christ”, 2 Corinthians 5: 19. What irresistible power, what effectiveness in service!
Men had to confess, “He hath done all things well”, Mark 7: 37.

These are remarkable references in Isaiah 42: 3, “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench—he shall bring forth judgment according to truth”. Was not the woman in John 4 a broken reed and a smoking flax? How
gently the Lord handled her, with what skill, and yet with what faithfulness, so that she was not broken or extinguished but set up as a vessel of the Holy Spirit and a worshipper of God.

Think of that bereaved household at Bethany in John 11. You might say almost broken, the character of a bruised reed. The Lord intervenes in the deepest sympathy and compassion. It says, “Jesus wept”. Yet withal divine power was there as the Lord said, “Lazarus, come forth”.

So, the word is, “Behold my servant”. The Father calls us to share His delight in Him; “Mine elect in whom my soul delighteth”. The Spirit would strengthen us, as we read the gospels and contemplate Jesus, to share the Father’s delight in His Servant. And thus may we be formed like Him. It says in verse 4, “He shall not faint nor be in haste”. Let us learn from Him. Some may be fainting, discouraged perhaps by smallness of numbers. What small numbers Jesus had! He says prophetically, “I have spent my strength for nought”, Isaiah 49: 4. The visible fruit of His toil was very small, but He did not faint and He was not in haste.

We are to learn from Jesus: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus”, Philippians 2: 5. Sometimes we are in haste. Sometimes we cannot wait. We need to contemplate “my servant” moving ever in relation to the Father’s will and in the power of the Holy Spirit.

Psalm 2 presents God’s King. “I have anointed my king”. This is very steadying. What confusion there is around; what powers of lawlessness and evil. This is a word of comfort and assurance—“I have anointed my king upon Zion”. How wonderful to be in the light of this and the present experience of it as translated into the kingdom of the Son of the Father’s love in the midst of a lawless world. So we anticipate the world to come and experience
what the kingdom is, “righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit”, Romans 14: 17.

We are in the light of the heading, up of all things in Christ. The kingdom is a very wonderful area, where the will of God prevails. It underlies all assembly experience. If I am not a subject and obedient person I shall never really enjoy assembly things. Worse than that, I shall bring in trouble among the brethren. But subject persons are a source of strength to the brethren; their wills have been broken, as was the will of Saul of Tarsus who was led by the hand into the city. He came into the kingdom. He had seen the glory of the King. Saul had said to Him, “Who art thou, Lord?” (Acts 9: 5), and the answer was, “I am Jesus”. How blessed to be in the kingdom and thus to be ready for the assembly.

Then we think of the millennial day, of which Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15: 25—“For he must reign until he put all enemies under his feet”. This is the full answer to Psalm 2. The King has already been anointed; that is the secret in our hearts, and we know the power of the kingdom. But it is shortly to be displayed publicly; all things are to be put under His feet. All other rule and authority will be annulled, everything brought into subjection to God’s King.

That is how time will finish up. It says, “Then the end”, that is, the end of all God’s operations in time, everything subjected to Christ and then “he gives up the kingdom to him who is God and Father”, and the Son Himself shall be placed in subjection to Him, that God may be all in all.

How wonderful to be in the secret of God’s purpose, His fixed purpose, to head up all things in the Christ, the things in the heavens and the things upon the earth. This is steadying and keeps us restful. Think of all the powers that
have risen up in history, and current powers of evil—what Paul speaks of in Ephesians 6: 12,

“principalities ... authorities ... the universal lords of this darkness”. The divine answer is, “I have anointed my king upon Zion”. So let us go forward, dear brethren, assured and steady and worshipful in the knowledge that all is safely in the hands of the Son. May God bless these thoughts to us.

Not even Bezaleel or any of the wise-hearted men could have made the curtains or the coverings as they ought to be if the women had not done the spinning properly. There might be many gifts in a meeting, and much spiritual material available, but if the sisters were gossips and tale-bearers there would be a poor result for God! Spinning is binding the fibres together so that when they are woven there is a firm texture. The New Testament speaks of building together and knitting together, and we have seen in the tabernacle the thought of loops, and clasps, and rings, and couplings—the idea of all being held together. And the spinning is what we may call the fundamental process; if that is not done right, nothing will be right. Every sister can do a little spinning—can do something in the direction of getting the saints drawn together in the appreciation of Christ. To say a word or bring an influence to bear that promotes this is a valuable service. What we appreciate in Christ will characterize us. The more I appreciate what He is as the heavenly One, the more heavenly I shall be. That is the ‘blue’, and it is so with the
other colours also. All that Christ is has to take form in the affections of saints, and they have to be held together in the appreciation of Him. No other bond has any divine value.
paragraphs.source: C. A. Coates (‘Outline of Exodus’, p.307)

paragraphs.text: It is a solemn word, “Remember the wife of Lot”, Luke 17: 32 … The Lord here is warning us against making the most of our lives here, and the danger of not being satisfied with what is necessary. Perhaps we want to make a show. That is, our lives are in this matter; we are making the most of the things of the world by the use of external things here. The Lord says that a man’s life does not consist in the things which he possesses, and so He warns us here,
“Whosoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it, and whosoever shall lose it shall preserve it”. That is christianity. That is the Lord’s way of pointing out a true disciple.

It would be out of keeping with the Lord’s mind if we should assume to be the collective thing; it would not be according to the truth. We are on individual lines now, in the public aspect; but after all, the principles hold—they are always workable; and the “two or three” of Matthew answers to our position. But if we lose sight of the whole church, failing to own the dreadful breakdown, we shall be only a sect, and we shall not have the Lord.
